If you create a flow log for a subnet or VPC, each network interface in that subnet or VPC is monitored. For more information, see Work with flow logs (Amazon VPC documentation).\\\\n\\\\nFlow log data for a monitored network interface is recorded as flow log records. A *flow log record* represents a network flow in your VPC. By default, each record captures a network IP traffic flow that occurs within an aggregation interval. Each record is a string with fields separated by spaces. A record includes values for the different components of the IP flow, for example, the source, destination, and protocol. When you create a flow log, you can use the default format for the flow log record, or you can specify a custom format. For more information, see Flow log record examples (Amazon VPC documentation).\\\\n\\\\nFlow logs don\\'t capture the following information:\\\\n\\\\n* Traffic generated by instances when they contact the Amazon Domain Name System (DNS) server. The VPC Flow Logs on the source instance don\\'t capture Traffic Mirroring data.\\\\n \\\\n2. Use the following CloudWatch Logs query to see the logs for your Traffic Mirroring data:\\\\n ```plaintext\\\\n fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, srcPort, dstPort, protocol\\\\n | filter protocol in [6, 17] # 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP\\\\n | filter srcAddr like \\'10.0.\\' # Filter for internal source IPs\\\\n | stats count(*) as requestCount by srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort\\\\n | sort requestCount desc\\\\n | limit 20\\\\n ```\\\\n \\\\n Example output:\\\\n \\\\n ```plaintext\\\\n 2 123456789012 eni-093c2d\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/vpc-traffic-mirroring-instance\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Flow log limitations\",\"context\":\"# Flow log limitations\\\\n\\\\nTo use flow logs, you need to be aware of the following limitations:\\\\n\\\\n* After you create a flow log, you won\\'t see flow log data until there is active\\\\n traffic for the network interface, subnet, or VPC that you selected.\\\\n* You can\\'t enable flow logs for VPCs that are peered with your VPC unless the\\\\n peer VPC is in your account.\\\\n* After you create a flow log, you can\\'t change its configuration or the\\\\n flow log record format. {"id": "83e741ca-483f-469f-88ae-86ecae8bb9e2", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "That's confirmed, and the answer is important: **no, it doesn't mean the queries are failing** — it means flow logs can't tell you either way.

VPC Flow Logs explicitly exclude traffic to the Amazon-provided DNS server (the VPC resolver). AWS documentation lists this as one of the things flow logs never capture, regardless of whether the traffic succeeds or fails. So an empty result for that traffic is expected behavior, not a sign of a problem — you'd see the same empty result whether DNS was working perfectly or totally broken.

To actually check if `i-0abc123def456789`'s DNS queries are succeeding, you'd want **Route 53 Resolver Query Logging** instead — it specifically captures queries sent to the VPC resolver, including the queried domain, the source instance, and the response received. Flow logs just aren't the right data source for this.

One exception worth noting: if the instance is configured to use a custom/self-managed DNS server rather than the Amazon-provided resolver, flow logs *would* capture that traffic — so it's also worth confirming which resolver the instance is actually configured to use.

Want me to help set up or check Route 53 Resolver query logging for that instance?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
